newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German markets nervous over Buba gold fight.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German markets nervous over Buba gold fight.

text.p: German financial markets will remain on edge in the near-term over Bonn's intentions to revalue Germany's gold reserves and the risk it could derail the push for a single European currency, traders said on Thursday.
Germany's cash debt market and IBIS computer share dealings were both open for business on Thursday despite the closure of bourse and futures markets for a regional holiday.

German markets that were opened showed a mixed reaction to the Bundesbank's objections to Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to plug budget holes with the gold revaluation to try to meet the economic conditions for European currency union membership.

Traders said debt markets were more likely to suffer on Friday from the uncertainity rather than the share market. Stocks have ironically benefited from dollar safe-haven buying since the weaker mark made export-sensitive shares more attractive.
"A lot of this has been built into the market but we could see some medium-term pressure," said Dirk Aufderheide, a trader at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Futures & Options in Frankfurt.
"The market is surprisingly stable but still nervous."
The IBIS DAX on Thursday was showing a rise of 7.79 points to 3,634.39 at 1240 GMT after reaching a high at 3,637.77 in very thin trade to match Wednesday's bourse close at 3,636.42 points.
German 10-year debt futures on the LIFFE exchange in London were down 36 basis points, or 0.36 percentage points, at 100.45 points at midday after earlier reaching a low at 100.33 in active trade.
The benchmark six percent 10-year cash Bund due July 2007 also slipped to 100.22 percent from 100.68 percent on Wednesday as the yield rose to 5.96 percent.

"The dealings are quite thin," Norman Beauchamp, senior trader at Co-operative Bank in London, told Reuters Financial Television. "People are also staying away because they are confused. That does not help much either."
The Bundesbank's anticipated objection to Bonn's plan had weighed on German markets in dealings on Wednesday when German financial markets ended steady to lower.
"It is difficult to see this being anything but bad news for bonds," said Holger Fahrinkrug, economist at Union Bank of Switzerland in Frankfurt.

"The dominant factor for now is uncertainity, not just in Germany but also in France, and this suggests that European markets as a whole are likely to come under further pressure, with the high-yielders particularly vulnerable."
Fahrinkrug said one could argue that if Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU) project was eventually postponed because of the Bundesbank-Bonn fight, then it would be supportive for debt prices.
But he also said a victory for Bonn would cement the start of monetary union with a broad base and would be good for convergence trades, namely through higher German yields.
Share market traders, however, expected the 30-share DAX index to remain relatively resilient despite the conflict.
"The market is holding on rather well," said Birgit Bachmann at BHF-Bank in Frankfurt. "I think the market has reacted so far relatively positively to the fight."
Bachmann said the Bundesbank showed "it was not willing to give up its historic stance and accept a weaker currency."
Traders also noted the share market has been buoyant even when the dollar recently fell under 1.70 marks and shrugged off losses in German debt futures in London.
"The German share market has shown that it can stand on its own legs," said one trader.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525
